title: Stem Anatomy and Vascular Transport
objective: Identify the stem tissues that support the canopy and transport water, minerals, sugars, and signals.

terms.definition: Vascular tissue that conducts water and dissolved minerals primarily from roots toward shoots.
Vascular tissue that distributes sugars and other transported compounds between sources and sinks.
A lateral meristem that contributes to secondary vascular growth.
Central stem tissue that can contribute to storage and internal structure.

coreScience: The cannabis stem is both a support column and a transport network. Epidermal and cortical tissues form the outer region of young stems. Vascular bundles contain xylem toward the interior and phloem toward the exterior, with cambial activity contributing to thickening as stems mature. The central region contains pith.

Xylem transport is driven largely by the water-potential gradient created as water evaporates from leaves. A continuous water column, root supply, and intact conducting tissue are required. Phloem moves photosynthates and other compounds from source tissues, often mature leaves, toward growing shoots, roots, flowers, and other sinks.

Bending or cutting a stem changes both mechanical loading and vascular continuity. Plants can reinforce injured areas through wound responses and new tissue, but severe crushing, splitting, constriction, infection, or repeated movement can reduce transport and create entry sites for pathogens.
cultivationRelevance: Support decisions should account for increasing flower mass and lever forces. Stem diameter alone does not guarantee resistance to splitting at branch junctions.
When diagnosing a wilted branch, compare the symptom boundary with the stem. A localized kink, girdle, lesion, or break points toward transport failure rather than a whole-root-zone problem.

measureAndRecord.requirement: Angle, included bark or crease, splitting, and support.
Location, length, depth, tissue discoloration, and date.
Whole plant, one branch, or tissue above an injury.
New growth, callus formation, continued wilt, or failure.

misconceptions: Xylem pumps water: Water movement depends largely on physical gradients and transpiration, supported by living root processes.
A healed-looking knuckle is always stronger: Appearance does not prove restored transport or resistance to future load.
All stem purple coloration is phosphorus deficiency: Pigmentation can reflect genetics, light, temperature, age, or stress and is not diagnostic alone.
evidenceLimits: Detailed stem anatomy varies with age, position, cultivar, and fiber-versus-drug selection. The tissue functions described here are the transferable baseline.
sourceNotes: Hesami M., Pepe M., and Jones A.M.P. (2023). Morphological Characterization of Cannabis sativa L. Throughout Its Complete Life Cycle. Plants 12(20):3646.
Savatin D.V., Gramegna G., Modesti V., and Cervone F. (2014). Wounding in the plant tissue: the defense of a dangerous passage. Frontiers in Plant Science 5:470.
